a: White has 20 possible first moves: 16 pawn moves and 4 knight moves. The engine rates the best of them as practically equal, each worth about a third of a pawn to White. That small edge is simply the advantage of moving first.

The two classical moves put a pawn in the centre straight away. [e4] is the most popular: it takes the centre and opens lines for the queen and the f1 bishop, and usually leads to open, tactical games, such as [e4 e5] or the Sicilian [e4 c5]. [d4] does the same with the queen's pawn, which the queen already protects. Its games tend to be more strategic, and its main road is the Queen's Gambit, [d4 d5 c4].

The engine's favourite by a hair is [Nf3], the Réti, which fights for the centre with a piece and stops ...e5. Like the English [c4], it keeps every option open and often transposes into 1.d4 openings, as in [Nf3 d5 d4]. After [c4 e5], White is playing a Sicilian with colours reversed and an extra tempo. [g3] and [b3] prepare to bring a bishop out on a long diagonal.

Then come modest moves that keep the balance but give up most of White's edge. [e3] and [d3] open only one bishop's diagonal, [c3] takes the c3 square from the knight, and [Nc3] blocks the c-pawn. Flank moves such as [a3], [h3], [b4], [a4] and [h4] do even less for the centre. Bird's Opening [f4] controls e5 but loosens White's king, which From's Gambit [f4 e5] tries to exploit.

The worst first moves harm White's own position. [Na3] and [Nh3] put a knight on the rim, where it controls few squares. [f3] takes the best square from the g1 knight and opens the e1–h4 diagonal to White's king, which leads to the fastest checkmate in chess, Fool's Mate: [f3 e5 g4 Qh4]. The engine's very worst is the Grob [g4], which loosens White's kingside for nothing: after [g4 d5], the c8 bishop already eyes the g4 pawn.

How far the engine looks changes its favourite. At depth 8 [e4] is clearly the best first move, worth +0.53, and [Nf3] and [d4] are only +0.26 and +0.23; at depth 16 [e4] has come down to +0.35, and at depth 25 to +0.29, while [Nf3] has grown to +0.37 and [d4] to +0.31. The three end up too close to separate, so the shallow search's preference for [e4] is an artefact of depth, not a real edge.

t: The Orthodox setup. The knight supports the freeing breaks ...c5 or ...e5. Black often plays ...c6, ...dxc4 and ...e5, or simplifies with ...Ne4.

a: Black has 20 possible replies. Four of them stand out, keeping White's edge to about a third of a pawn according to the engine. The classical [d5] stops 2.e4 for good and invites the Queen's Gambit with [d5 c4]. [Nf6] does the same job with a piece: it stops 2.e4 without committing a pawn, and leaves Black free to choose between the Indian defences, such as the King's Indian with [Nf6 c4 g6] or the Nimzo-Indian with [Nf6 c4 e6 Nc3 Bb4].

The quiet [e6] and [c6] are just as good. Both prepare ...d5 while keeping options open: after [e6], White's [e6 e4] turns the game into a French Defence, and after [c6], [c6 e4] leads to a Caro-Kann, while [c6 c4] brings a Slav.

A second group is sound but more committal, at around two-thirds of a pawn for White. The Dutch [f5] grabs e4 with a pawn and aims for kingside play, at the cost of loosening Black's king, which the sharp Staunton Gambit [f5 e4] tries to exploit. [g6] and [d6] let White build a big centre and plan to undermine it later, often transposing into a King's Indian. The Old Benoni [c5] and the Mikenas [Nc6] attack d4 straight away, but White usually answers by gaining space with tempo: [c5 d5] or [Nc6 d5].

Flank moves give White a free hand in the centre. [b6] and [b5] prepare ...Bb7 to fight for e4 from a distance, for example [b6 e4 Bb7 Bd3]. [a6] is a waiting move preparing ...b5. [Na6] and [Nh6] put a knight on the rim, and [h6], [a5] and [h5] do nothing for the centre or development.

Three replies are simply bad. [f6] takes the best square from the g8 knight and weakens the e8–h5 diagonal to Black's king. The Englund Gambit [e5] gives away a pawn after [e5 dxe5], hoping for tricks such as [e5 dxe5 Nc6 Nf3 Qe7 Bf4 Qb4], which hits both the bishop and b2. Worst of all, the Borg Gambit [g5] just drops a pawn to [g5 Bxg5]: about two pawns for White.

The best replies are steady across depths: [Nf6], [d5] and [e6] stay between -0.18 and -0.35 from Black's side at depths 8, 16 and 25, and [c6] climbs from -0.49 at depth 8 to -0.29, level with [Nf6]. The move a shallow search overrates is the English [b6]: at depth 8 it looks almost as good as [Nf6] (-0.32), but it costs almost a pawn at depth 16 (-0.98) and depth 25 (-0.87).

t: Pins the knight to the queen, indirectly increasing the pressure on d5.
The Exchange Variation. White clarifies the pawn structure immediately, aiming for the minority attack (b4–b5) later.
Black recaptures with the e-pawn, which also opens the diagonal for the c8 bishop.
Develops with a pin, pressuring f6 and indirectly d5.
Reinforces d5 and opens the d8–a5 diagonal for the queen. This is the Carlsbad structure, one of the most important to understand.
Solid, opening the way for the light-squared bishop.
Breaks the pin calmly. Black prioritises solidity and quick castling.
Opens the way for the f1 bishop and supports d4.
Black castles: the king is safe and the rook can join the game.
Natural development, controlling e5.

a: White has 27 moves here, and two of them keep White's full opening edge. The Queen's Gambit [c4] attacks d5 at once and asks Black to decide about the centre: take with [c4 dxc4], hold with [c4 e6] or [c4 c6], or counter-attack with [c4 e5]. [Nf3], the Zukertort, is almost as good and more flexible: it develops, keeps an eye on e5, and can still turn into a Queen's Gambit with c4 a move later.

Many players prefer a system they can set up against anything. The London [Bf4] brings the dark-squared bishop out before e3 shuts it in. [e3] prepares the Colle or the Stonewall, with Bd3, Nd2 and sometimes f4. [c3] supports d4 and keeps the queen's diagonal to b3 open, and [g3] prepares a fianchetto in the style of the Catalan. These moves keep the balance rather than fight for an advantage: the engine rates them all between equal and +0.2.

Sharper players look for an early fight. [Nc3] develops but blocks the c-pawn; after [Nc3 Nf6 Bg5] it becomes the Veresov. The Levitsky [Bg5] develops the bishop with a hit on e7 straight away. Both are about equal. The Blackmar-Diemer Gambit [e4] goes further and gives up a pawn for quick development: after [e4 dxe4 Nc3 Nf6 f3], White hopes to open the f-file against Black's king, but the engine prefers Black by more than half a pawn. The Mason [f4] grabs e5 but weakens e4 and the diagonal to White's king.

The rest give Black the easier game. Early queen moves such as [Qd3] (the Amazon Attack) and [Qd2] get in the way of White's own bishops. [Bd2] and [Be3] develop the bishop to passive squares, the last one in front of the e-pawn. Flank moves such as [a3], [h3], [b3], [a4], [h4] and [b4], and the knight moves to the rim [Na3] and [Nh3], do little for the centre.

A few moves are real mistakes. [f3] takes the best square from the g1 knight and weakens the king, and [Kd2] blocks the bishop and the queen with the king itself. The Zurich Gambit [g4] simply drops a pawn to [g4 Bxg4]. Worst of all, [Bh6] gives a whole bishop away to [Bh6 gxh6].

The Queen's Gambit is a move the engine appreciates more the deeper it looks: [c4] is only +0.15 at depth 8, +0.32 at depth 16 and +0.38 at depth 25. [e3] goes the other way, the shallow search's favourite at +0.44 and only +0.15 at depth 25, and the London [Bf4] ends at +0.06 after +0.15 and +0.22. The Blackmar-Diemer Gambit [e4] looks like a pawn lost at depth 8 (-0.98) and costs about half a pawn deeper (-0.51), while [h4] looks harmless at depth 8 (-0.11) and costs half a pawn at depth 25 (-0.48).

t: The Queen's Gambit, known since the 15th century. White offers the c-pawn to pull Black's d-pawn away from the centre so White can play e4. It is not a real gambit: the pawn can almost always be regained.

a: The Queen's Gambit. The c4 pawn attacks d5, and Black has to decide what to do about the centre. Three answers stand out, and the engine cannot separate them: each leaves White the usual edge of about a third of a pawn. The Queen's Gambit Declined [e6] holds d5 with a pawn and keeps a rock-solid centre, but it shuts in the c8 bishop for a while. The Slav [c6] holds d5 just as firmly while keeping that bishop's diagonal open. The Queen's Gambit Accepted [dxc4] takes the pawn and gives up the centre for a moment in exchange for free development; White wins the pawn back, for instance with [dxc4 e3] followed by Bxc4, and trying to keep it with ...b5 backfires, as in [dxc4 e4 b5 a4].

Black can also hit back instead of defending. The Austrian [c5] strikes at d4 in return, but after [c5 cxd5 Qxd5 Nc3] Black's queen is chased around the board. The Chigorin [Nc6] develops pieces rather than defending with pawns, often pinning the f3 knight later with ...Bg4. The Albin Countergambit [e5] sacrifices a pawn for activity after [e5 dxe5 d4]. All three are playable but give White more than the main lines, around half a pawn to two-thirds.

Some developing moves forget to look after d5. The Marshall [Nf6] lets White take the centre with tempo: [Nf6 cxd5 Nxd5 e4]. The Baltic [Bf5] develops the bishop before ...e6, but leaves b7 undefended, which [Bf5 Qb3] attacks at once; the engine prefers [Bf5 cxd5]. [g6] prepares ...Bg7, but after [g6 cxd5 Qxd5 Nc3] the queen is again a target. These cost Black between two-thirds of a pawn and a pawn.

The weaker moves all give White a free hand in the centre, at more than a pawn. Queen moves such as [Qd6] and [Qd7] block Black's own bishops, and [Nd7] and [Bd7] do the same. [Be6] stands in front of the e-pawn. [Bg4] takes the bishop away from the queenside while d5 still needs support, and the engine's answer is again [Bg4 cxd5], worth almost two pawns to White. Flank moves such as [a6], [h6], [a5], [h5] and [b6] do nothing for d5, [f5] and [f6] loosen Black's king, and [Na6] and [Nh6] put a knight on the rim.

A few moves simply lose material or time. The Zilbermints Gambit [b5] gives a pawn away to [b5 cxb5], and [g5] drops one to [g5 Bxg5]. [Kd7] blocks the queen and the light-squared bishop with the king itself, at more than three pawns. Worst of all, [Bh3] gives the bishop away to [Bh3 gxh3].

The three main defences hold up at depth: at depth 25 [e6], [c6] and [dxc4] are -0.29, -0.32 and -0.34 from Black's side. The shallow search underrates the Slav [c6], -0.56 at depth 8, while [e6] and [dxc4] are already around -0.30 there. The Albin [e5] does best at depth 16, -0.48, and slips back to -0.69 at depth 25. The move that fools a shallow search most is [Bd7]: at depth 8 it looks about as good as the Marshall [Nf6] (-0.79), but it costs a pawn and two-thirds at depth 25. [Nh6] is similar, -1.07 at depth 8 and almost two pawns deeper.

t: Queen's Gambit Accepted. Black grabs the pawn, giving up the centre for a moment in exchange for free development.
Queen's Gambit Declined. Black supports d5 with a pawn and keeps a firm foothold in the centre. The price: the c8 bishop is temporarily locked in.
Black supports d5 with the c-pawn and keeps the c8–h3 diagonal open, solving the QGD's main problem.
Black answers a gambit with a gambit, sacrificing the e-pawn for quick activity. Objectively a bit dubious, but White needs to know what to do.
Develops and adds pressure on d5.
Black defends d5 a second time while developing.
Breaks the pin.
The bishop takes aim at h7 and Black's kingside.
Black develops; later regroupings like ...Nf8 and ...Ne6 or ...Ng6 are typical.
Flexible development.
Now Black takes, threatening to keep the pawn with ...b5.
Develops and controls e4.
Adds pressure on d5.
Stops ...b5 so White can win the pawn back. The cost: the b4 square is weakened.
The point of the Slav: the light-squared bishop gets out before ...e6 closes it in.

a: Black is a pawn up, with a pawn on c4, and the question is how White wins it back. The pawn on c4 is hard to keep for long: once the e-pawn moves, the f1 bishop attacks it. The engine's favourite is the Central Variation [e4] (Saduleto in the lichess list), which takes the whole centre and opens the bishop's diagonal in one go. Black has to react at once, usually by striking back with [e4 e5]. Trying to keep the pawn with [e4 b5] runs into [e4 b5 a4], as the lines below show.

The Normal Variation [Nf3] and the Old Variation [e3] are calmer and almost as good. [Nf3] develops first and stops ...e5; the classical main line continues [Nf3 Nf6 e3 e6 Bxc4]. [e3] opens the bishop at once, and Black's most direct answer is [e3 e5].

[Nc3] and the Mannheim [Qa4+] only keep the balance. The knight on c3 does not attack c4, so Black can answer [Nc3 a6] and prepare ...b5 to hold the pawn. [Qa4+] wins the pawn back quickly with Qxc4, but brings the queen out very early.

Moves that do nothing about c4 leave Black a healthy extra pawn, at around half a pawn to a pawn for Black: bishop moves such as [Bf4], [Bg5], [Bd2] and [Be3], the slow [g3], [a3], [h3], [h4], [a4] and [f4], or [Nd2], [Qd2] and [Qc2]. [f3] prepares e4 but takes the best square from the g1 knight, [Na3] puts a knight on the rim, and [d5] pushes past without winning the pawn back.

Watch the c4 pawn: it attacks b3 and d3. So [b3] only gives it a target to take, [b3 cxb3], and [b4] allows it to capture en passant, [b4 cxb3], leaving Black two pawns up. Worst of all, [Qb3] and [Qd3] put the queen where that pawn takes it: [Qd3 cxd3]. Other mistakes are [g4], which drops a pawn to [g4 Bxg4], [Nh3], [Kd2], and [Bh6], which gives a bishop away to [Bh6 gxh6].

t: White builds an ideal pawn centre straight away and plans to win back c4 later.
A flexible developing move that also prevents ...e5, Black's most natural central break.

a: White has built the ideal centre and is ready to win back c4 with Bxc4. The score table has no depth-25 scores for this position, so the scores here were computed on the spot: at depth 20 for the six main replies, at depth 16 for the rest.

Two replies share first place and keep White's edge to under half a pawn. The Alekhine System [Nf6] attacks e4 at once; White usually gains space with [Nf6 e5 Nd5], and the knight finds a good central square. The McDonnell Defence [e5] strikes back at the centre before White has finished developing, as in [e5 Nf3 exd4 Bxc4]. The Modern Defence [Nc6] is just behind, putting pressure on d4 straight away.

[e6] and the Rubinstein Defence [c5] are a little less precise: [e6] frees the f8 bishop and prepares ...c5, while [c5] hits d4 at once. Holding the pawn with the Greco Variation [b5] is close too, but only if Black knows what comes next. White's best answer is [b5 a4], hitting the base of the pawn chain, and from there [b5 a4 a6] walks into a trap, while [b5 a4 c6 axb5 cxb5 Nc3] keeps White pressing.

Slower moves give White a pawn's worth or more. [a6], [g6] and [c6] take time without challenging the centre, and [c6] also takes the c6 square from Black's own knight. [Nd7], [Bd7] and [Be6] develop to passive squares; the bishop on e6 can be chased by [Be6 d5]. Queen moves such as [Qd6] and [Qd7] invite White's pieces to gain time, flank moves such as [a5], [b6], [h6] and [h5] do nothing for the centre, and [Na6] and [Nh6] put a knight on the rim. The Schwartz Defence [f5] and [f6] loosen Black's king, and [c3] simply gives the pawn back: [c3 bxc3].

The rest lose material. [g5] drops a pawn to [g5 Bxg5] and [Kd7] blocks Black's own pieces with the king. [Bg4] hangs the bishop to [Bg4 Qxg4], [Bf5] to [Bf5 exf5], and [Bh3] to [Bh3 gxh3]. Worst of all, the queen cannot join the fight yet: [Qxd4] grabs a pawn but loses the queen to [Qxd4 Qxd4], and [Qd5] loses it to [Qd5 exd5].

t: Black tries to keep the extra pawn by protecting c4. Greedy and risky: it weakens the queenside.
The most direct reply: Black hits back at the centre before White has finished developing.

a: Black has protected c4 with ...b5 and hopes to stay a pawn up. The score table has no depth-25 scores for this position, so the scores here were computed on the spot: at depth 20 for the six main moves, at depth 16 for the rest.

White has one clearly best answer, worth more than half a pawn more than anything else: [a4], which attacks the b5 pawn at once, at the base of Black's chain. Black cannot simply keep everything. Defending with [a4 a6] walks into a trap on the a-file, and [a4 c6] holds b5 for now, but after [a4 c6 axb5 cxb5 Nc3] White keeps hitting it.

Every other move lets Black keep the extra pawn in peace, and the engine rates them as equal at best for White. Natural developing moves such as [Nf3], [Nc3], [Be2] and [Ne2] are the most reasonable of them. [b3] attacks the chain from the other side, an idea that works later in the line, but here it comes too early. Slower moves such as [Be3], [Bg5], [Bf4], [Bd2], [g3], [a3], [h3], [h4], the pushes [e5] and [d5], or early queen moves like [Qc2] and [Qd2], give Black a comfortable extra pawn. [f3], [f4], [g4], [Qe2], [Qf3], [Qh5], [Na3], [Nh3], [Nd2], [Ke2], [Kd2] and [b4] are worse still.

Watch out for Black's two pawns, which protect each other and cover b3, d3 and a4. The natural [Bxc4] loses the bishop, since b5 guards c4: [Bxc4 bxc4]. [Bd3] puts the bishop where the c4 pawn takes it: [Bd3 cxd3]. The queen cannot come out either: [Qa4] walks into [Qa4 bxa4], [Qb3] into [Qb3 cxb3], [Qd3] into [Qd3 cxd3], and [Qg4] into [Qg4 Bxg4]. [Bh6] gives the bishop away to [Bh6 gxh6].

t: Attacks the base of the pawn chain right away.

a: White hits the b5 pawn, the base of Black's chain. The score table has no depth-25 scores for this position, so the scores here were computed on the spot: at depth 20 for the six main replies, at depth 16 for the rest. Whatever Black does, White's edge grows to at least three-quarters of a pawn: holding on to c4 is getting harder.

Three replies share the top. [c6] props up b5 with another pawn and is the main line: after [c6 axb5 cxb5] the b5–c4 chain survives, but [c6 axb5 cxb5 Nc3] keeps hitting b5, and [c6 axb5 cxb5 b3] attacks the chain from the other side. [Bb7] gives up b5 and goes after e4 instead: after [Bb7 axb5 Bxe4], Black is still a pawn up for the moment, but White leads in development. [Nf6] also counter-attacks e4.

Around a pawn for White come [b4], which pushes past but leaves c4 without support, so White wins it back with Bxc4, and quiet moves such as [Nd7], [e6], [Bd7], [e5] and [Nc6]. [Ba6] defends b5 from the side, but the bishop is passive there. [bxa4] gives up the chain altogether and leaves c4 hanging to the f1 bishop, and [c3] simply gives the pawn back: [c3 bxc3].

The natural-looking [a6] is a trap for Black. After [a6 axb5], recapturing with [a6 axb5 axb5] opens the a-file, and [a6 axb5 axb5 Rxa8] wins the rook. Even without that blunder, the engine gives White more than one and a half pawns. Slow moves such as [a5], [c5], [h6], [g6], [h5], [Na6] and [Nh6], queen moves like [Qd6] and [Qd7], and [g5], [f5], [f6], [Be6] and [Kd7] are even worse.

The rest lose material at once: [Bg4] hangs the bishop to [Bg4 Qxg4], [Bf5] to [Bf5 exf5], and [Bh3] to [Bh3 gxh3]. The queen still cannot come out: [Qxd4] loses it to [Qxd4 Qxd4], and [Qd5] to [Qd5 exd5].

t: Black props up b5 with another pawn.
Defends b5 with the a-pawn, but this opens the a-file once the pawns are exchanged. 4...c6 was the way to keep b5 protected.

a: Black has defended b5 with the a-pawn, which looks natural but creates a weakness on the a-file. The score table has no depth-25 scores for this position, so the scores here were computed on the spot: at depth 20 for the six main moves, at depth 16 for the rest.

White has one good move, and it is worth more than one and a half pawns more than anything else: [axb5]. Material is level again, and Black cannot take back. Recapturing with [axb5 axb5] opens the a-file, and [axb5 axb5 Rxa8] wins the rook, which nothing defends: the knight on b8 and the bishop on c8 block the queen. Black does better to leave the pawn alone, as in [axb5 e6] or [axb5 Bb7], but the engine still gives White about one and a half pawns: the pawn on b5 stays, and the a6 pawn is tied to the defence of the a-file.

Any other move lets Black off the hook, and the engine rates them as equal at best for White. The developing moves [Nf3], [Be2] and [Nc3] and the push [e5] are the most reasonable, and [b3] attacks the chain from the wrong side. Slower moves such as [d5], [Bd2], [Be3], [Bf4], [Bg5], [Ne2], [Nh3], [Nd2], [g3], [h4], [f3], [f4], [Ra2], or early queen moves like [Qc2] and [Qd2], give Black a comfortable extra pawn. [g4], [h3], [Qe2], [Qh5], [Qf3], [Na3], [Ke2], [Ra3], [b4] and [Kd2] are worse still, and [a5] gives up the attack on b5 for good.

The same pawn tactics as before punish the natural bishop and queen moves: [Bxc4] loses the bishop to [Bxc4 bxc4], [Bd3] to [Bd3 cxd3], and [Bh6] to [Bh6 gxh6]. [Qb3] walks into [Qb3 cxb3], [Qd3] into [Qd3 cxd3], and [Qg4] into [Qg4 Bxg4].

t: White takes, inviting the natural recapture.

a: Material is level. The score table has no depth-25 scores for this position, so the scores here were computed on the spot: at depth 20 for the six main replies, at depth 16 for the rest.

Black now has two problems. The pawn on b5 cannot be taken back, because that would open the a-file to the rook on a8. And the c4 pawn has lost its protector, so White threatens to win it with Bxc4 and be a pawn up. Black cannot solve both, and every reply leaves White at least one and a half pawns better.

The best Black can do is accept it and develop. [Nf6], [e6] and [Bb7] are practically equal: the knight and the bishop both hit e4, and [e6] opens the way for the f8 bishop. None of them saves c4, as in [e6 Bxc4]. [c6] hits b5 a second time and [h6] waits, but both cost almost another pawn, as do [e5], [a5] and [Nd7].

The natural recapture is the real blunder: [axb5] opens the a-file, and [axb5 Rxa8] wins the rook, which nothing defends. [Nc6] is just as bad, since the b5 pawn takes it: [Nc6 bxc6]. Slow moves such as [g6], [h5], [Ra7], [Nh6], [c5], [Be6], [Bd7], [g5], [f6], [f5], queen moves like [Qd6] and [Qd7], [c3] and [Kd7] leave White three or four pawns ahead. The rest lose material at once: [Bg4] to [Bg4 Qxg4], [Bf5] to [Bf5 exf5], [Bh3] to [Bh3 gxh3], [Qd5] to [Qd5 exd5], and [Qxd4] to [Qxd4 Qxd4].

t: The natural recapture, and a blunder: the a-file is now completely open.

a: The two rooks face each other down the open a-file. Whoever moves first takes the other, and it is White's turn. The score table has no depth-25 scores for this position, so the scores here were computed on the spot: at depth 20 for the six main moves, at depth 16 for the rest.

[Rxa8] wins a whole rook, worth four and a half pawns according to the engine. Nothing can take back: the knight on b8 and the bishop on c8 stand between Black's queen and a8. The rook on a8 even attacks the knight on b8 next, and nothing defends that either.

Every other move throws the trap away. After any natural developing move, Black's rook takes White's instead, as in [Nf3 Rxa1], and Black ends up five pawns or more ahead. Moving the rook up the file does not help: on a2, a5, a6 or a7 the black rook simply takes it, and on a4 the b5 pawn does. Only two moves save the rook. [Ra3] is protected by the b2 pawn, and [Na3] blocks the file. But both leave Black the extra c4 pawn, and the engine then prefers Black by more than a pawn and a half.

t: The rook sweeps down the open file and wins Black's rook on a8. Nothing defends it: the knight on b8 and the bishop on c8 block the queen. White is winning.

a: White has won a rook and is about four and a half pawns up. The score table has no depth-25 scores for this position, so the scores here were computed on the spot: at depth 20 for the six main replies, at depth 16 for the rest.

Black's first problem is the knight on b8: the rook attacks it, and nothing defends it, because the bishop on c8 still blocks the queen. White threatens to take it next. The best answer is [Bb7], which clears c8 so that the queen now guards b8, and at the same time attacks the rook on a8 and the e4 pawn. White's rook has to leave a8, and Black gets a little activity back. [Bd7], [Ba6] and [Be6] also open the queen's path to b8, but do less. Moving the knight away works too: [Nd7] is the best of those, ahead of [Nc6] and [Na6].

Everything else loses the knight as well, as in [e6 Rxb8], leaving White six pawns or more ahead: [c6], [e6], [e5], [Nf6], [h6], [g6], [h5], [Nh6], [f5], [c5], [g5], [f6], [Kd7], [c3], or queen moves like [Qd7] and [Qd6] that do not defend b8. [Bf5], [Bg4] and [Bh3] free c8 but put the bishop where it can be taken. [b4] also gives up the c4 pawn to the f1 bishop. Worst of all, [Qd5] and [Qxd4] lose the queen: [Qd5 exd5], [Qxd4 Qxd4].

t: White trades on b5…
…and Black keeps the b5–c4 chain together.
Develops with a threat: the knight attacks b5, which no longer has a pawn defending it. Black has to spend another move on the queenside while White keeps developing.
Another way to punish ...b5: attack the chain from the other side. If c4 is exchanged, b5 is left hanging.
Black takes, but now the b5 pawn has no support.
White wins the pawn back with check. With the c- and d-pawns gone, the diagonal to e8 is wide open.
Blocks the check.
Material is level again, and White has the ideal e4–d4 centre and a big lead in development. Black's greed has backfired.
Black defends b5 with the a-pawn. The same weakness as in the ...a6 trap appears: if this pawn ever recaptures on b5, the a-file opens for White's rook.

The knight takes the pawn anyway. If 7...axb5??, the a-file opens and 8.Rxa8 wins the rook, which nothing defends. If Black leaves the knight alone, White has simply won a pawn and the knight is strongly placed on b5.
Develops and defends d4.
Black removes White's d-pawn, so White's centre is down to the e4 pawn.
White wins back the gambit pawn and points the bishop at f7. Black is temporarily a pawn up (d4), but White leads in development.
Protects d4 and develops.
White castles quickly. The lead in development is the compensation for the d4 pawn.
Black challenges the strong bishop on c4.
White trades, doubling Black's e-pawns.
Black accepts doubled pawns in return for the half-open f-file.
A double attack on b7 and e6.
Defends e6. After 9.Qxb7 Rb8 10.Qa6, Black gets active play on the b-file in return for the pawn.
Black develops and keeps an eye on e4.
White regains the pawn with a lead in development. The bishop is well placed, eyeing e6 and f7.
The key freeing move: Black strikes at d4 so White cannot build an unchallenged centre.
Opens the f1–a6 diagonal so the bishop can recapture on c4.
Solid: frees Black's dark-squared bishop and supports a later ...c5.
King safety first. White prepares Qe2, Rd1 and central play with e4 or dxc5.
Prepares ...b5 to gain queenside space with tempo on the bishop, and gives the c8 bishop a future on b7.

a: The Chigorin Defence of the Queen's Gambit. Black develops pieces rather than holding d5 with pawns: the knight already presses on d4, and the c8 bishop is free to come out, often to pin a knight on f3 with ...Bg4. The score table has no depth-25 scores for this position, so the scores here were computed on the spot: at depth 20 for the six main moves, at depth 16 for the rest.

Four moves keep White's edge of about half a pawn, and the engine cannot separate them. [Nc3] develops and adds pressure on d5. [cxd5] attacks the knight with the new d5 pawn, so Black takes back with the queen, [cxd5 Qxd5], and White gains time against it with [cxd5 Qxd5 Nc3]. [e3] protects d4 and opens the f1 bishop. [Nf3] protects d4 too, and Black's typical answer is [Nf3 Bg4], pinning the knight.

Quieter moves give away most of White's edge. [Bf4] and [h3], which stops ...Bg4, keep a small plus. [h4], [Bg5], [g3] and [Qa4], which pins the c6 knight, are about equal. [a3], [Bd2], [Na3], [f4], [Qd2], [Be3], [c5], which releases the pressure on d5, [Nh3], [Nd2], [a4], [f3], [b3] and [b4] give Black the easier game.

Watch d4 and e4. The knight attacks d4 and only White's queen defends it, so [Qc2] and [Qb3] leave it to [Qc2 Nxd4], and [Kd2] blocks the queen's defence with the king. [Qd3] and [Qb3] also run into ...dxc4, after which the pawn on c4 attacks the queen: [Qd3 dxc4]. [e4] simply hangs a pawn: [e4 dxe4]. [g4] loosens White's kingside for nothing, and [Bh6] gives the bishop away to [Bh6 gxh6].

The Albin Countergambit. Black offers the e-pawn to open lines and, after it is taken, to drive the d-pawn to d4, where it cramps White's position. White has 31 moves, and one of them is clearly best.

Accepting with [dxe5] is the engine's choice by half a pawn, +0.79: White wins a pawn and Black has to prove the activity is worth it. At depth 14 Black's best replies, [dxe5 Ne7], [dxe5 dxc4] and the classical [dxe5 d4], are all about two-thirds of a pawn to a pawn behind.

Declining keeps less. [Nc3] develops and adds pressure on d5, +0.29, and [cxd5] takes the other pawn, +0.21. [e3] gives up most of the edge, and [Nf3] runs into [Nf3 e4], which chases the knight. [a3], [h3], [Qa4+], [Qd2], [g3], [h4], [Be3], [e4], [a4], [Bd2], [Na3], [Nd2], [Qb3], [Nh3], [Qc2] and [f3] all leave Black the better game, between a third of a pawn and a pawn and a quarter.

Some moves weaken White badly: [b3], [g4], [Qd3], which runs into [Qd3 dxc4], [c5], [f4], which gives a pawn to [f4 exf4], and [b4], which gives one to [b4 Bxb4+]. Three bishop moves lose the bishop: [Bg5] to [Bg5 Qxg5], [Bf4] to [Bf4 exf4] and [Bh6] to [Bh6 Nxh6]. Worst of all is [Kd2], putting the king in front of its own pieces in the open centre.

[dxe5] is the best move at every depth, +0.79 to +0.88 for White, and [Nc3] and [cxd5] stay well behind it. The move whose score depends most on depth is [Kd2]: three pawns for Black at depth 8, four at depth 16, more than five at depth 25. [b4] also gets worse the deeper one looks, from -1.83 to -2.63.

t: White accepts.
The point: this pawn cramps White, taking away c3 and e3 from White's pieces.
Best. White develops calmly. The natural-looking 4.e3? falls into the Lasker Trap.
Natural-looking, but a mistake: White tries to break up the d4 pawn and walks into a trap.

Forced.

8.Rxg1 runs into 8...Bg4+, skewering the king and winning the queen on d1.
The attack crashes through. White's king is stuck in the centre.
The king runs.
Another piece joins the attack, with ...Bg4 and ...Rd8+ coming. Black is winning.
Black develops and attacks the e5 pawn.

Whatever Black plays, White mates: in one move after [c4], [d4] or [f4], and in two after [c6].

The Vienna Game. White's knight covers d5 and e4 and leaves the f-pawn free, so f4 is often White's next idea. It does not attack e5, and Black has two replies that leave White practically nothing, the engine giving White +0.04 and +0.12.

[Nc6] develops and defends e5, ready to meet [Nc6 f4] with ...exf4, or the Bishop's Opening set-up [Nc6 Bc4] with ...Nf6. [Nf6] counter-attacks e4 instead. White can then play the Vienna Gambit [Nf6 f4], take aim at f7 with [Nf6 Bc4], or keep it quiet with [Nf6 Nf3].

The bishop moves are a little less accurate. The Anderssen [Bc5] aims at f2 and stops d4 for the moment, and [Bb4] pins nothing yet but prepares to take on c3; both give White about a third of a pawn. [d6] is solid but passive, [Be7] and [Bd6] develop to modest squares, the second blocking the d-pawn, and [c6] prepares ...d5 slowly: all between half a pawn and two-thirds.

Slow pawn moves such as [a6], [h6], [c5] and [a5], the knight move [Ne7] and early queen moves such as [Qe7] and [Qf6] cost more. [d5] opens the centre too early, as after [d5 exd5] White's knight is already pointing at d5, and [b6], [h5], [g6] and [Nh6] do little. [f6] takes the knight's square and loosens Black's king, and [f5] gives a pawn to [f5 exf5].

The early queen raids lose time: [Qh4] is met by [Qh4 Nf3], and [Qg5] by [Qg5 d4], which develops a piece and hits e5 while attacking the queen; both are about two pawns for White. [Na6] puts the knight on the rim, [b5] drops a pawn to [b5 Nxb5], [g5] loosens the kingside, [Ke7] gives up castling, and [Ba3] gives a bishop away to [Ba3 bxa3].

Depth changes the order of the best moves. At depth 8 the shallow search prefers [Bc5] and [Nc6], both around +0.23 for White, and rates [Nf6] at +0.52. By depth 16 [Nf6] is already +0.13, and depth 25 confirms it at +0.12 while [Bc5] slips to +0.37: the counter-attack on e4 needs depth to be appreciated. [Be7] and [c6] are the opposite of tricky: they look like more than a pawn for White at depth 8 and only about half a pawn deeper.

A symmetrical position: both knights on c3 and c6, both e-pawns defended. White has 31 moves and the position is level: the best keep about a tenth of a pawn, and a dozen more are within a tenth of equality.

[Bc4] puts the bishop on its most active diagonal, aiming at f7; after [Bc4 Nf6] the game is a Stanley Variation, and [Bc4 Bc5] mirrors it. [Nge2] keeps f4 free and [Nf3] turns the game into a Three Knights. [a4], [h3], the Paulsen [g3], [a3], [Bd3], [Rb1], [d3], [Nd5], [Bb5] and [Be2] are all within a tenth of a pawn of equality.

The gambits are a little worse: [f4] offers a pawn to [f4 exf4], and the Fyfe Gambit [d4] gives the centre pawn after [d4 exd4], a third to two-thirds of a pawn for Black. [h4], [b3], [Nh3], the queen moves [Qf3] and [Qe2], and [f3] are slow or awkward, about half a pawn.

The worst moves undo White's development or weaken the king: the knight moves [Na4], [Nce2], [Nb5] and [Nb1], the queen raids [Qh5] and [Qg4], and [g4], [Ke2] and [b4], which gives a pawn to [b4 Nxb4], are worth about a pawn to Black. [Ba6] gives a bishop to [Ba6 bxa6].

The depths disagree on the top moves without changing the verdict. At depth 8 [Nf3] is the best at +0.43, and settles at +0.07 at depth 25. [Bd3] looks like most of a pawn for Black at depth 8 (-0.78) and is about equal at depth 16 and 25. The trickiest is [Nb5]: almost four pawns for Black at depth 8, under a pawn at depth 16 and 25.

a: White's bishop aims at f7, the square only Black's king defends, and with that bishop on c4, nothing defends g2. Black has 31 moves, and two of them keep the position level.

[Nf6] is the engine's best, rated exactly equal at depths 8, 16 and 25: it develops, attacks e4 and covers h7, and reaches the Three Knights line of the Stanley Variation. [Bc5] mirrors White's bishop and is almost as good, +0.13 for White.

Solid but passive moves cost about a third of a pawn: [h6], [d6], [a5], [a6], [Be7] and [g6]. [Nd4], [Rb8], [Bd6], which blocks the d-pawn, [f5], which opens the diagonal to Black's king, [Nge7], [Bb4], [Na5], [b6], [Nh6] and [Qe7] give White half a pawn to a pawn.

Some moves weaken Black or waste time: [Qf6], [h5], [Nb4], [d5], which gives a pawn after [d5 Bxd5], [g5], [Nce7], [f6], which takes the knight's square and opens the diagonal to the king, [b5], which gives a pawn to [b5 Bxb5], [Nb8] and [Ke7]. The queen raids [Qh4], which hits e4, and [Qg5], which hits g2, come out too early, a pawn and a half for White. [Ba3] gives the bishop to [Ba3 bxa3].

Three moves change a lot with depth. [Bb4] is nearly equal at depth 8 (+0.17) and most of a pawn worse at depth 25 (+0.84), and [Bc5] dips to +0.37 at depth 16 before coming back to +0.13.

a: Black's knight attacks e4, which White's knight defends. White has 31 moves, and none of them keeps more than a sixth of a pawn.

[Nf3] is the engine's choice, +0.16, and turns the game into a Three Knights. The Mieses [g3] prepares to fianchetto the bishop, and the Stanley [Bc4] aims at f7; both are rated equal. The Vienna Gambit [f4] strikes at e5 at once, and is about equal too (-0.09): after [f4 d5] Black hits back in the centre, which is the gambit's main line.

Quiet moves such as [h3], [a3], [Be2], [d4], [a4], [Nge2], [Bd3], [d3] and [Rb1] keep the balance, within a fifth of a pawn. [Bb5], [Nd5], [Qe2] and [Qf3] are a little worse, about four-tenths to half a pawn, the queen moves bringing the queen out before the minor pieces.

[Nh3], [f3], [h4], [b3] and [g4] cost more, [Nb5] wanders, and the retreats [Nb1], [Nce2] and [Na4] undo White's development, as does [Ke2] the right to castle. [b4] gives a pawn. Three moves lose material: [Ba6] gives the bishop to [Ba6 Nxa6], and the queen raids [Qh5] and [Qg4] land on squares the f6 knight covers, [Qh5 Nxh5] and [Qg4 Nxg4].

Two moves are not what they seem at shallow depth. [d4] looks like White's best by far at depth 8, +0.70, but it is about equal at depth 16 (-0.09) and slightly worse at depth 25 (-0.16). [f4] goes the other way: -0.33 at depth 8, +0.01 at depth 16, -0.09 at depth 25, so the shallow search underrates the gambit.

a: The Vienna Gambit. White's f-pawn attacks e5 and threatens fxe5, which would also hit the f6 knight. Black has 28 moves, and only three of them deal with that well; most of the others lose a lot.

The best is the counter-attack [d5], which the engine rates slightly in Black's favour (+0.20 for Black). It opens the centre while White's king stands in the middle: after [d5 fxe5 Nxe4] the knight jumps into the centre, and the engine sees the position as level. [d6] holds e5 with a pawn and is solid, +0.37 for White. Taking the gambit with [exf4] is playable, +0.51, but after [exf4 e5 Ng8] the knight has to go back home.

Everything else lets fxe5 hurt. [Nc6] develops but the knight is chased after [Nc6 fxe5 Nxe5 d4], giving White a pawn and a half. [Qe7], [b5], [h5], [h6], [Ng8], [Bb4], [g6] and [a6] cost about two pawns, [Nxe4] gives the knight for a pawn after [Nxe4 Nxe4], and the bishop moves [Be7], [Bd6] and [Bc5] leave the knight to be hit by [Bc5 fxe5]. [c6], [c5], [a5], [Na6], [b6], [g5], [Rg8], [Ke7], and the knight moves [Ng4], [Nd5] and [Nh5] cost three to five pawns, and the bishop to [Ba3 bxa3].

This is the trickiest position of the line for a shallow search. At depth 8 [exf4] looks like a blunder, nearly two pawns for White (-1.83 for Black), but at depth 16 it is -0.44 and at depth 25 -0.51: taking the pawn is fine, but its defence takes depth to see. [d5] is equal at depth 8 and 16 and only becomes Black's best at depth 25 (+0.20), while [d6] is -0.33 to -0.37 at every depth.

a: The Sicilian. Black's c-pawn watches d4 from the side, so the centre is unbalanced at once. White has 30 moves, and the best group keeps an edge of between a sixth and two-fifths of a pawn, closer together than the table can separate.

[Nf3] is the main road, preparing d4 with a knight behind it: after [Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4] or [Nf3 Nc6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4] the open Sicilians begin. The Closed Sicilian [Nc3] keeps the centre closed and often follows with g3 and Bg2 or with f4. The Alapin [c3] prepares d4 with a pawn so that White can take back on d4 with a pawn. The Keres [Ne2] and the Staunton-Cochrane [c4] are rarer, and [d4] at once offers the Smith-Morra Gambit [d4 cxd4 c3], a pawn for quick development.
[c4] puts a second pawn beside e4, so that d5 is covered twice, but it gives up d4 for good: no white pawn can attack that square any more, and a black knight can settle there, as after [c4 Nc6].

Many moves keep the balance without trying for more: [Be2], [h3], [a4], [g3], [Na3], [Bb5], [a3], the Bowdler [Bc4], the McDonnell [f4], [Bd3], [d3], [b3] and [h4], all between +0.16 and -0.17. [Bc4] aims at f7, but the bishop runs into ...e6 and ...d5.

The rest give Black the better game. Early queen moves such as [Qh5], [Qe2], [Qf3] and the Amazon [Qg4] get in the way and can be chased. [f3] takes the knight's square, [Nh3] puts the knight on the rim, the Wing Gambit [b4] offers a pawn to [b4 cxb4], and [e5] advances before the pawn can be supported. [Ke2] gives up castling and the Grob [g4] loosens the kingside, both about a pawn. [Ba6] gives a bishop away to [Ba6 Nxa6].

Three moves are worth watching across depths. [d4] looks like White's best by far at depth 8, +0.85, but deeper it is only +0.27 and then +0.16. The Keres [Ne2] goes the other way: about equal at depth 8 (+0.04), it climbs to +0.37 at depth 16 and +0.29 at depth 25. [Nc3] also starts high, +0.56 at depth 8, and settles at +0.26 at depth 16 and +0.28 at depth 25.

a: White's knight on f3 now covers d4 and e5. d4 is still a square no white pawn can attack, and it is contested one for one: the knight against Black's pawn on c5. Black has 28 moves, and the engine keeps White's edge small only with the best of them, about a sixth of a pawn; the next ones already give White close to half a pawn.

[Nc6] is the engine's choice. It adds a second guard to d4 and prepares to occupy it: after [Nc6 Nc3 Nd4] the knight stands on the square no pawn can drive it from, and [Nc6 d4 cxd4] is White opening the centre instead. [Nf6] and [b6] come next, and the table cannot separate [Nf6] from [Nc6]. [Nf6] attacks e4 but can be chased: after [Nf6 e5 Ng8] the knight is back home, and [Nf6 e5 Ng4] runs into [Nf6 e5 Ng4 h3]. [b6] prepares ...Bb7 against e4, as in [b6 Be2 Qc7].

A group of quieter moves costs half a pawn to three quarters: the queen moves [Qb6], [Qc7], [Qa5] and [Qf6], the waiting moves [h6], [a6] and [h5], and the developing [Be7], [Ne7] and [d6]. [Bd6] and [Qe7] are a little worse, since each stands in front of a pawn or a piece that still has to move.

[d5] strikes at the square both white pawns cover, and it is answered by [d5 cxd5 exd5 exd5]: White comes out a pawn up. [e5] simply loses a pawn to [e5 Nxe5], since nothing defends e5 against the knight, and [b5] loses one to [b5 cxb5]. [f5], [f6], [g6], [g5] and the king walk [Ke7] loosen Black's king, each by more than a pawn.
Two queen moves lose the queen at once, because the knight on f3 covers both squares: [Qh4] to [Qh4 Nxh4], and [Qg5] to [Qg5 Nxg5].

The shallow search misjudges [d5] most: at depth 8 it is Black's second-best move, costing only a fifth of a pawn (-0.23 from Black's side), but at depth 25 it costs -0.82. [Nf6] goes the other way, from -0.82 at depth 8 to -0.40 at depth 25, while [Nc6] is the best move at both depths.

a: The Closed Sicilian. White's knight covers d5 and keeps the option of g3 and Bg2, or of f4, without opening the centre. Black has 22 moves, and six of them leave White the usual third of a pawn, too close for the table to separate.

[Nc6] is the Traditional line and the engine's best, +0.30 for White: it covers d4 and e5 and keeps every structure open. [e6] prepares ...d5, [d6] supports ...e5 or a fianchetto, [g6] prepares ...Bg7 along the long diagonal, which the Closed Sicilian often mirrors on both sides, [a6] prepares ...b5, and [Qc7] watches e5.
[b6], [h5], [Qb6], [Nf6], [h6], [e5] and [Qa5] are less flexible, between six-tenths of a pawn and nine-tenths. [Nf6] invites [Nf6 e5], which chases the knight.

The rest give White a pawn or more: [Nh6] and [Na6] are on the rim, [d5] opens the centre to [d5 exd5], [f5] gives a pawn to [f5 exf5], [f6] takes the knight's square, [b5] gives one to [b5 Nxb5], [g5] and [a5] weaken, and [c4] simply drops the c-pawn to [c4 Bxc4].

Two of the best moves look bad at shallow depth. At depth 8, [g6] and [Qc7] seem to cost well over a pawn (+1.37 and +1.32 for White); from depth 16 on they are as good as the rest of the best group, +0.36 and +0.39 at depth 25. [d6] goes the other way: the best at depth 16 (+0.18), it falls back to +0.41 at depth 25.

Two white pawns stand side by side on c4 and e4. Together they cover d5 twice, but they have passed d4 and d3, so no white pawn can ever attack those squares again, and Black's pawn on c5 already watches d4. Black has 21 moves, and the engine finds five of them within a fifth of a pawn of equality, too close for the table to separate.

[Nc6] heads for that hole: a knight that reaches d4 cannot be chased away by a pawn, and the c5 pawn supports it there. [Nc6 Nc3 g6 g3 Bg7 Bg2] is the English Opening's Botvinnik System, with the g7 bishop aiming at d4 as well. [e5] puts a second black pawn on d4's guard and mirrors White's structure, a closed game about the squares d4 and d5; the engine goes on with [e5 d3 Nc6]. [d6] keeps the e-pawn back for now, and [d6 Nc3 Nc6 g3 h5] is the Gloria Variation.

[e6] and [Nf6] develop towards the centre. [e6] opens the f8 bishop and prepares ...d5; after [e6 Nf3 Nc6 d4 cxd4] White trades the d-pawn to open the centre. [Nf6] attacks e4 and is chased by [Nf6 e5]: [Nf6 e5 Ng8] goes back home with an even game, but [Nf6 e5 Ne4] runs into [Nf6 e5 Ne4 d3], and the knight on e4 has no safe square left.

The queen moves come next, each worth a third of a pawn or a little more to White: [Qa5], [Qb6], which eyes b2, and [Qc7] bring the queen out before any minor piece. [b6] prepares ...Bb7 against e4. The waiting moves [h6], [a6] and [g6] cost about six tenths of a pawn, [h5] and [Nh6] a little more.

The worst moves give a pawn away or do nothing for the centre. [d5] strikes at the one square both white pawns cover: [d5 cxd5] wins a pawn, and after [d5 cxd5 e6 Bb5+] White is still a pawn up with the bishop giving check. [b5] loses one to [b5 cxb5] and [f5] to [f5 exf5]. [f6] and [g5] loosen Black's king, and [a5] and [Na6] leave the centre alone; each of these is worth about a pawn to White.

The shallow search ranks several moves differently. At depth 8 [e5] is Black's best, a little better than equal (+0.12 from Black's side), and [a6] third (-0.02), but at depth 25 [a6] costs more than six tenths of a pawn. [Nf6] goes the other way: -0.48 from Black's side at depth 8, -0.18 at depth 25, level with [e6]. [d5] is the worst move at depth 8 (-2.10) and next to worst at depth 25 (-1.27), just ahead of [b5].

a: White's pawns stand on c4 and e4, Black's on c5 and e6. The e6 pawn opens the f8 bishop's diagonal and the queen's road to h4, and it covers d5 once, against White's two pawns there; d4, which no white pawn can attack any more, is still watched by the c5 pawn. White has 28 moves and is close to level: the best of them is worth a fifth of a pawn, and only the first three keep any edge at all.

The knights come first. [Nf3] and [Nc3] are too close for the table to separate, and both are usually met by the knight that heads for d4: [Nf3 Nc6 Nc3 Nd4] and [Nc3 Nc6 Nf3 Nd4] lead to the same position. [Nf3 Nc6 d4 cxd4] opens the centre instead, and [Be2] is the quiet way to prepare castling.

Opening the centre at once is no improvement. [d4] is answered by [d4 cxd4], and after [d4 cxd4 Qxd4] White's queen is out early; once [d4 cxd4 Qxd4 Nf6] is played, Black is the side with the edge. [e5] runs ahead of its support: [e5 d6] attacks the pawn straight away, it cannot be held, and Black ends up about a pawn better.

Most of the pawn moves, [h3], [a3], [a4], [g3], [b3], [d3] and [h4], and the developing [Bd3] and [Ne2] cost between a tenth and a third of a pawn. The early queen moves [Qe2], [Qa4], [Qb3], [Qc2], [Qg4], [Qh5] and [Qf3] cost up to a pawn, [Qc2] most of one: after [Qc2 Nf6] the knight already presses on e4.

The worst moves cost more than a pawn. [Ke2] gives up castling and blocks the f1 bishop. [b4] offers a pawn and opens the long diagonal to the rook on a1: after [b4 Qf6] the queen attacks the rook and the b4 pawn is still loose.

The shallow search likes the fianchetto more than it should: at depth 8 [g3] is third, worth +0.42, but at depth 25 it gives Black the edge (-0.20). [d4] also drops, from equal at depth 8 to -0.13, while [Nc3] (+0.47 at depth 8) and [Nf3] (+0.43) end up at +0.13 and +0.20.

a: Black's knight on c6 and pawn on c5 both watch d4, against White's one knight on f3, so Black is ready to put the knight there. White has 26 moves; only the best keeps a small edge, a sixth of a pawn, and the engine cannot separate it from the two that follow, which are about level.

[d4] removes the square before Black can use it: after [d4 cxd4 Nxd4] White's knight stands in the centre and the game is even, and [d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6] is the engine's way on. The other two keep the centre closed and let the knight come: [Nc3] covers d5 a third time, and [Be2] prepares castling without blocking anything.

The waiting moves [h3], [g3], [a3], [d3] and [a4] cost up to a quarter of a pawn, [b3], [h4] and [Na3] about a third, and the early queen moves [Qe2], [Qa4], [Qc2] and [Qb3] between two fifths and two thirds.

[Bd3] is clearly worse than [d4], by four fifths of a pawn: the bishop stands in front of the d-pawn, so d4 can no longer be played and the c1 bishop stays shut in. The engine answers [Bd3 Be7], meaning ...Bf6 next, aiming the bishop at d4 too.

[e5] pushes a pawn that the c6 knight already attacks, and it costs a pawn's worth. [Rg1] and [Ng1] undo White's development, and [g4] loosens the kingside; [b4] gives a pawn to [b4 Nxb4], and [Ke2] gives up castling.
Four knight moves lose the knight outright: [Ne5] to [Ne5 Nxe5], [Ng5] to [Ng5 Qxg5], [Nh4] to [Nh4 Qxh4] and [Nd4] to [Nd4 cxd4]. With e7 empty, Black's queen reaches g5 and h4 along the diagonal.

The shallow search rates [Nc3] best by a clear margin, +0.39 at depth 8, but at depth 25 it is level (-0.03) and [d4] is first. [b4] looks almost harmless at depth 8 (-0.47) and costs well over a pawn deeper (-1.36).

The knight is lost to [Ng4 Qxg4].
The bishop is lost for a pawn to [Bxh2+ Kxh2].
The knight is lost to [Nh5 Qxh5].
The knight is lost to [Nd5 cxd5].

a: The French Defence. Black's pawn on e6 prepares ...d5, which will challenge e4 with a pawn the e6 pawn supports. The cost is that the c8 bishop's diagonal is shut for the time being.

[d4] is clearly White's best, +0.43: it takes the whole centre while it is free, and after [d4 d5] the main French begins, with White choosing between defending, advancing or exchanging the e4 pawn. [Nc3] and [Nf3] develop first and are a little behind, +0.25 and +0.20; after [Nc3 d5] White can still play d4.

Many moves keep about equality without fighting for the centre: [h3], the Réti-Spielmann [g3], [Be2], the Steiner [c4], the King's Indian Attack [d3], [c3], the Chigorin [Qe2], [Bd3], [a3], the Bird Invitation [Bb5], the La Bourdonnais [f4] and the Steinitz [e5], which advances before d4 can support the pawn.

The rest give Black a little: [a4], [h4], [Ne2], [Nh3], [Qf3], the Horwitz [b3], [Bc4], which runs into ...d5, [f3], [Na3], and the queen moves [Qg4] and [Qh5], from a fifth of a pawn to a half. [g4], the Banzai-Leong Gambit [b4], which gives a pawn to [b4 Bxb4], and [Ke2] cost about a pawn, and [Ba6] gives the bishop away to [Ba6 Nxa6].

[d4] is White's best at every depth, +0.44 at depth 8, +0.52 at depth 16 and +0.43 at depth 25. [Be2] is the move a shallow search overrates: at depth 8 it looks as good as [d4] (+0.46), but deeper it is only equal. [Nf3] goes the other way, from -0.05 at depth 8 to +0.20, and the Steiner [c4] from -0.36 to equality.

The Caro-Kann. Black's pawn on c6 prepares ...d5, which will challenge e4 with a pawn the c6 pawn supports. White has 30 moves, and a broad group of them keeps an edge of about a third of a pawn: the engine's figures for [Nc3], [d4], [f3], [Nf3], [d3] and [c4] lie between +0.22 and +0.39, too close for the table to tell apart.

[d4] is the main road: it takes the whole centre while it is free, and after [d4 d5] White has to decide how to deal with the attack on e4. [Nc3] defends e4 with a piece first, and after [Nc3 d5 Nf3] the game is the Two Knights Attack. [Nf3] develops and waits for [Nf3 d5]. [f3] supports e4 in advance with a pawn, and after [f3 d5 d4] the game reaches the Maróczy Variation. The Accelerated Panov [c4] prepares to meet ...d5 by taking on d5, and the Breyer [d3] is a quiet set-up in which e4 is held by a pawn.

Many modest moves keep the balance without fighting for more, between +0.17 and -0.03: [a3], [c3], [h3], [Be2], [Na3], [a4], [Bd3], [Ne2], [h4], [Qf3], [g3] and [f4]. The advance [e5] gains space while Black's d-pawn is still at home, but it gives up most of White's edge.

The weaker moves cost White something. [Qe2] stands in front of the f1 bishop, and the Euwe [b3] is slow. The Hillbilly [Bc4] puts the bishop on the very diagonal ...d5 is about to close: after [Bc4 d5 exd5 cxd5] the bishop is attacked and has to move again, while Black has a pawn on d5, which is why the engine gives Black about four-tenths of a pawn. The Labahn [b4] loosens the queenside, the early queen moves [Qg4] and [Qh5] come out to be chased, [Nh3] puts a knight on the rim, the Spike [g4] weakens White's kingside, and [Ke2] gives up castling for nothing. [Bb5] and [Ba6] simply give a bishop away, to [Bb5 cxb5] and [Ba6 Nxa6].

The depth of the search matters here. At depth 8, [c3], [Nc3], [f3] and [Nf3] all look worth two-thirds of a pawn or more, and [c3] is the shallow search's favourite at +0.78; deeper, they settle around a third, and [c3] falls to +0.17. [c4] holds up a little longer, still +0.45 at depth 16, before dropping to +0.22 at depth 25. [d4] is the steady one: +0.29, +0.25 and +0.36 at depths 8, 16 and 25, so its value does not depend on how far one looks.

White has both centre pawns side by side, and Black's pawn on c6 is there to support ...d5. [d5] is by far the best move: it strikes at e4 with a pawn the c6 pawn supports, and keeps White's edge to about a fifth of a pawn. After [d5 Nc3] or [d5 e5] the game is a main line of the Caro-Kann.

Everything else lets White keep the big centre for free, and the gap is wide: the next best moves, [d6] and [a6], already give White more than half a pawn. [g6] and [e6] prepare a fianchetto or ...d5 a move later, and [Qa5+] and [Qb6] bring the queen out early. The De Bruycker [Na6], [Nh6] and the slow pawn moves [a5], [h6], [b6] and [h5] cost about a pawn.

The Masi [Nf6] attacks e4, but the knight is chased at once by [Nf6 e5]. Some pawn moves just give a pawn: [c5] to [c5 dxc5], [b5] to [b5 Bxb5], [e5] to [e5 dxe5], the Massachusetts [f5] to [f5 exf5], and [g5] to [g5 Bxg5], the worst of all at two and a half pawns. [f6] costs no pawn but takes the knight's square and loosens Black's king.

The shallow search is too pessimistic about [d5]: it gives White +0.60 at depth 8, then +0.26 at depth 16 and +0.22 at depth 25. Nothing changes the verdict, though: at every depth [d5] is the best move by a clear margin.

The main position of the Caro-Kann. Black's d-pawn attacks e4, which nothing defends, so White's first job is to decide about that pawn: defend it, push it past, exchange it, or let it go. White has 38 moves, and only a handful keep the opening edge.

The best answers defend e4 with a knight. [Nc3] and [Nd2] are the engine's top two, at about half a pawn, and both are usually met by [Nc3 dxe4 Nxe4], where the knight recaptures on a good central square. The Advance [e5] pushes the pawn past the attack and gains space, at the cost of giving Black's light-squared bishop the f5 square, as in [e5 Bf5]. The Maróczy [f3] holds e4 with a pawn. The Exchange [exd5] releases the tension: after [exd5 cxd5] the pawn structure is symmetrical, which keeps only a small edge, +0.17.

Defending e4 with another piece keeps the balance, but no more: [Bd3] and the queen moves [Qe2], [Qd3] and [Qf3] are all about equal, the queen moves putting the queen where a minor piece wants to go. [Ne2] does not defend e4 at all and is about equal too.

Every other move ignores e4, and Black can simply take it, as in [Nf3 dxe4], after which the knight is attacked as well. That costs White between four-tenths and nine-tenths of a pawn: [h3], [c3], [g3], [a3], [Bg5], [Bf4], [g4], [a4], [Nh3], [h4], [Nf3], [Qd2], [Na3] and [Be2]. The Mieses Gambit [Be3] and the Diemer Gambit [c4] give e4 on purpose, for development or a second central pawn, and are no better.

[b3], [Bd2], [b4] and [f4] lose more than a pawn, the last because [f4 dxe4] also leaves White's king's diagonal open. [Qh5] comes out to nothing, and [Ke2] and [Kd2] block White's own pieces with the king. Five moves give a piece away: [Bc4 dxc4], [Bb5 cxb5], [Ba6 Nxa6], [Bh6 Nxh6], and worst of all the queen to [Qg4 Bxg4].

The scores move with the depth more than in most positions. At depth 8, [e5] (+0.67) and [Nc3] (+0.62) lead, and [exd5] looks worth +0.47; at depth 25, [exd5] has fallen to +0.17, so the shallow search overrates the exchange. [Nc3] dips to +0.24 at depth 16 before coming back to +0.49, while [Nd2] only grows, from +0.27 to +0.45. And the moves that let e4 go look harmless at first: [c3] is +0.08 at depth 8 and [c4] -0.04, but both cost about half a pawn deeper, -0.45 and -0.63. Giving up the e-pawn takes depth to punish.

White's knight defends e4, and the tension in the centre is Black's to resolve. One move stands far above the rest: [dxe4] gives up the centre pawn for a moment to take White's, and after [dxe4 Nxe4] Black can develop with ...Bf5, ...Nd7 or ...Nf6. The engine gives White only +0.12.

Every other move keeps the tension and lets White decide it, at a cost of at least six-tenths of a pawn. [h6], [a6] and [e6] are the least bad; [e6] turns the game into a French-like structure in which the c6 pawn is misplaced. The Gurgenidze ideas [g6] and [b5], early queen moves such as [Qa5], [Qd7], [Qd6], [Qb6] and [Qc7], and developing moves that block Black's own pieces, [Be6], [Nd7] and [Bd7], all give White most of a pawn or more. The Campomanes [Nf6] runs into [Nf6 e5], which chases the knight.
Some moves weaken Black for good. [f6] and [g5] loosen the king, and [c5] gives up the c6 pawn's support of d5, so that [c5 exd5] wins a pawn. [Kd7] blocks the queen and the bishop with the king.

Three bishop moves simply lose the bishop. [Bf5] is taken by [Bf5 exf5], [Bh3] by [Bh3 gxh3], and [Bg4] by [Bg4 Qxg4], the queen's diagonal to g4 being open since e2 is empty. After [Bg4], White must not answer [Bg4 exd5], which gives the queen away to [Bg4 exd5 Bxd1].

[dxe4] is best at every depth, and the shallow search even makes it look worse than it is (+0.27 for White at depth 8, +0.12 at depth 16 and 25). The tricky one is [Bg4]: at depth 8 it costs only about two and three-quarter pawns, but by depth 16 and 25 the bishop is simply lost, more than five pawns.

Black's pawn stands on e4, and White is a pawn down. [Nxe4] takes it at once and is the only move that keeps White's edge, +0.43: the knight comes to the centre, and the main lines go on with [Nxe4 Bf5], [Nxe4 Nd7] or [Nxe4 Nf6].

[Nge2] is the only other move that keeps the balance, aiming to take on e4 with a knight a move later, from g3 or c3. The gambits are a step down: the von Hennig [Bc4] develops first and leaves the pawn, and the Rasa-Studier [f3] offers a second pawn after [f3 exf3], both about half a pawn for Black.

Everything else simply leaves White a pawn down: [h3], [a3], [Qd2], [Bg5], [g4], [a4], [Be3], [Bf4], [h4], [g3], [Be2], [Qe2], [Nce2], [Rb1], [Nh3], [Bd2], [Qh5], [b3], [Nb1], [b4] and [Na4], between four-tenths and a pawn and a half. [d5] gives a second pawn to [d5 cxd5], [Ke2] and [Kd2] put the king in the way, and [f4] allows [f4 exf3], taking en passant and opening White's king.

Many moves give a piece away. [Nf3] and [Bd3] land on squares the e4 pawn attacks, as in [Nf3 exf3] and [Bd3 exd3]; [Bb5] and [Nb5] are taken by the c6 pawn, [Bb5 cxb5]; [Bh6] by [Bh6 Nxh6], [Ba6] by [Ba6 Nxa6], and [Nd5] by [Nd5 cxd5]. The queen moves [Qf3], [Qd3] and [Qg4] give the queen itself, the last to [Qg4 Bxg4].

[Nxe4] grows with depth: +0.28 at depth 8, +0.24 at depth 16, +0.43 at depth 25. [Nge2] looks a third of a pawn worse than equal at depth 8 (-0.33) and is about equal deeper; [h3] starts at a full pawn for Black and settles at four-tenths.
The main line of the Caro-Kann. White's knight stands in the centre, and Black has three classical ways to go on, all about a third of a pawn behind and too close for the table to separate.

The Classical [Bf5] develops the light-squared bishop outside the pawn chain with a hit on the knight, and after [Bf5 Ng3 Bg6] it settles on g6. The Karpov [Nd7] prepares ...Ngf6 so that a knight exchange on f6 can be met by a knight. [Nf6] challenges the e4 knight straight away: after [Nf6 Nxf6+] Black chooses between ...exf6 and ...gxf6, both leaving the pawns damaged.

A second group costs a little more, between half a pawn and nine-tenths: the fianchetto [g6], the Finnish [h6], [a6], the queen moves [Qd5], [Qc7], [Qb6] and [Qa5+], and [Na6], [Be6], [e6] and [Bd7]. [e6] in particular shuts in the c8 bishop, whose diagonal is open.

[h5], [Nh6], [b5], [b6], [Qd7] and the pawn breaks [c5] and [e5], which White can meet with [c5 dxc5] or [e5 dxe5], cost from one to one and two-thirds pawns. [f6], [f5] and [g5] loosen Black's king, and [Kd7] blocks Black's queen and bishop. The rest give material away: [Bg4] to [Bg4 Qxg4], [Bh3] to [Bh3 Nxh3], [Qd6] to [Qd6 Nxd6], and [Qxd4] the queen to [Qxd4 Qxd4].

Which of the three is best depends on the depth. At depth 8 the shallow search prefers [Nf6] by far, giving White only +0.11, ahead of [Nd7] (+0.54) and [Bf5] (+0.57). At depth 16 [Bf5] leads at +0.26 and [Nd7] trails at +0.63; at depth 25 [Nd7] is the engine's best at +0.32, [Bf5] +0.36 and [Nf6] +0.42. None of the three is a mistake.
Black's knight attacks the one on e4, which nothing defends. White has 42 moves, and 34 of them lose the knight, so the first question is simply what to do with it.

Exchanging is best: [Nxf6+] is the engine's choice at +0.37, and Black has to decide how to take back, [Nxf6+ exf6] keeping the king safe behind a healthy kingside, or [Nxf6+ gxf6] taking the open g-file at the cost of the structure. Defending or moving the knight keeps the balance and no more: [Qd3] defends it, [Ng3], [Nc3] and [Nc5] retreat or step aside, all between +0.13 and -0.03. The Alekhine Gambit [Bd3] defends it too, but the bishop blocks the queen's defence of d4, which Black can take with [Bd3 Qxd4]; [f3] defends it with a pawn and [Ng5] steps out of the way. All three are about a fifth of a pawn for Black.
Three moves save the knight but give up d4. [Nd2] retreats into the queen's path to d4, and [Qf3] and [Qe2] take the queen off the d-file, so that [Qe2 Qxd4] wins a pawn: about a pawn for Black.

Everything else ignores the knight and loses it: [h3], [c3], [Nf3] or [Be3], for example, are all answered by [h3 Nxe4]. [Nd6+] gives it up with check to [Nd6+ exd6], and the queen moves [Qh5] and [Qg4] put the queen where the f6 knight takes it, [Qg4 Nxg4].

[Nxf6+] is best at every depth, but the shallow search overrates it (+0.75 at depth 8, +0.37 at depth 16 and 25). The other knight moves drift closer to equal as the search goes deeper: [Ng3] is +0.28 at depth 8 and +0.06 at depth 25, and [Nc5] goes from -0.33 to -0.03.

The Advance Variation. White's pawn on e5 gains space and takes f6 from Black's knight, and the pawn chain d4-e5 points at Black's kingside. In return the chain shuts nothing in on Black's side: the light-squared bishop can still come out, and the chain can be attacked at its base with ...c5.

The two classical answers do exactly that. [Bf5] develops the bishop outside the pawn chain before ...e6 closes its diagonal, and is the engine's best, +0.25 for White. The Botvinnik-Carls [c5] strikes at d4 at once, a little behind at +0.39. [e6] prepares ...c5 too, but shuts in the c8 bishop, which leaves White about half a pawn.

The rest are slower: [Bd7], the queen moves [Qc7], [Qb6] and [Qa5+], [a6], [g6], [Nh6], [h6], [a5], [h5], [f6], [Be6], [b6], [Na6], [Qd7], [b5] and [Nd7] cost between seven-tenths of a pawn and a pawn and a quarter. [f5], [Kd7] and [g5] weaken Black's king.
Four moves lose material. [Nf6] puts the knight where the e5 pawn takes it, [Nf6 exf6]; [Bg4] is taken by [Bg4 Qxg4] and [Bh3] by [Bh3 gxh3]; and [Qd6] gives the queen to [Qd6 exd6].

[Bf5] gains with depth (+0.58, +0.35, +0.25 for White at depths 8, 16 and 25), and [c5] less so (+0.51, +0.41, +0.39). The move that fools a shallow search is [Be6]: at depth 8 it looks like more than two pawns for White, at depth 16 and 25 it is a pawn at most, slow but not losing.

m.n: Caro-Kann Defense: Advance Variation, Botvinnik-Carls Defense

a: The Botvinnik-Carls Defence of the Advance Variation. Black's pawn on c5 strikes at d4, the base of White's pawn chain, and none of Black's pieces is developed yet. White has 38 moves, and four of them keep a quarter to two-fifths of a pawn.

[Nf3] is the engine's best, +0.40: it defends d4 with a piece and develops. Taking with [dxc5] is almost as good, +0.36: White wins the pawn and gives up the base of the pawn chain. [c4] strikes at d5 in return, and [c3] supports d4 with a pawn, both about a quarter of a pawn.

[Bb5+], [Nc3], [f4], [Nd2], [Ne2], [Bf4], [Na3], [h3] and [Bd3] are close to equal, and [Be3] a little worse. Slow moves such as [a3], [a4], [b3], [h4], [Qd3], [Be2], [Qh5], [b4], [g3], [Bd2], [f3], [Qd2], [Bg5] and [Qf3] give Black a fifth of a pawn to six-tenths.

[e6] gives a pawn to [e6 Bxe6], [Qe2] blocks the f1 bishop, [g4] and [Nh3] loosen the kingside, and [Ke2] and [Kd2] give up castling. Four moves give material away: [Bc4] to [Bc4 dxc4], [Ba6] to [Ba6 Nxa6], [Bh6] to [Bh6 Nxh6], and the queen to [Qg4 Bxg4].

Two of the most natural moves are overrated by a shallow search. At depth 8 [dxc5] looks like a pawn for White (+0.96) and [c3] almost as much (+0.77); at depth 25 they are +0.36 and +0.21. [Nf3] is steadier, +0.52, +0.50 and +0.40 at depths 8, 16 and 25, and ends up the best. [h3] is the oddest: -0.13 at depth 8, the best of all at depth 16 (+0.34), and equal at depth 25.

White's pawn stands on d5, and Black is a pawn down. [cxd5] is the natural and best way to take it, +0.25 for White: the pawn structure becomes symmetrical, with one centre pawn each on d4 and d5 and an open c-file for Black, and the game goes on with [cxd5 Bd3], [cxd5 c4] or [cxd5 Nf3].

Everything else costs at least half a pawn more. [Qa5+] and [Qxd5] win the pawn back with the queen, but the queen in the centre is a target, as in [Qxd5 Nc3]. [Nf6] plans to take on d5 with the knight a move later. [Bf5], [a6], [g6], [e5], [e6] and the rest leave White a pawn up for now, between a pawn and a quarter and two pawns.

The worst moves add a weakness to the missing pawn: [f6], [f5], [b5], [g5] and [c5], and [Kd7], which puts the king in front of its pieces. Three bishop moves give the bishop away: [Bg4] to [Bg4 Qxg4], [Bh3] to [Bh3 Nxh3], and [Be6] to [Be6 dxe6].
There is nothing tricky here: [cxd5] is best at depth 8, 16 and 25, between +0.21 and +0.26 for White, and the next best moves stay about half a pawn behind at every depth.

The Exchange Variation. The pawn structure is symmetrical, one centre pawn each on d4 and d5, with the e-file open for White and the c-file for Black. Nothing is attacked, and White's edge is small whatever White plays: the best moves keep about a quarter of a pawn.

[c3] and the Panov [c4] are the engine's best, +0.29 and +0.27. [c3] supports d4 with a pawn and keeps the structure, the classical way to play the Exchange; [c4] attacks d5 at once and leads to open positions, often with an isolated pawn. [Bd3] and [Nf3] develop first, +0.17 and +0.13, and [Bd3] keeps an eye on h7.

A long list of moves is about equal: [Be3], [h3], [Ne2], [Bf4], [Nc3], [Bg5], [Be2], [Bb5+], [Qd3], [a4] and [Nd2]. Then come slower moves, [a3], [h4], [Na3], [g3], [Bd2], and early queen moves such as [Qd2], [Qf3], [Qe2] and [Qh5], between a tenth of a pawn and half a pawn for Black.

[b3], [f3], [b4] and [f4] loosen White's position, the Bulla Attack [g4] gives a pawn to [g4 Bxg4], [Nh3] goes to the rim, and [Kd2] and [Ke2] give up castling, about a pawn. Four moves give material away: [Bc4] to [Bc4 dxc4], [Ba6] to [Ba6 Nxa6], [Bh6] to [Bh6 Nxh6], and the queen to [Qg4 Bxg4].

The order of the best moves depends on the depth. At depth 8 [c4] leads (+0.39) and [c3] is only sixth (+0.15); at depth 16 [c3] falls to +0.09, well behind [c4], [Nf3] and [Bd3], and at depth 25 it is the best at +0.29. [Qd3] looks like half a pawn for Black at depth 8 and is equal at depth 25.

m.n: Caro-Kann Defense: Exchange Variation, Bulla Attack

a: A symmetrical pawn structure: one centre pawn each on d4 and d5, and open e- and c-files. Nothing is under attack, and Black has a wide choice of developing moves that keep White's edge to a fifth of a pawn or less.

[Bf5], [Nc6] and [Nf6] are the engine's best, +0.12 to +0.20 for White, too close to separate. [Bf5] develops the light-squared bishop before ...e6 shuts it in, [Nc6] puts pressure on d4, and [Nf6] covers e4 and prepares to castle. [Bg4] pins the f3 knight, a little behind at +0.34.

Quieter moves cost a little more: [a6], [e6], [h6], [Be6], [g6] and [Bd7] are between a third and half a pawn. The early queen moves [Qd6], [Qc7], [Qa5+] and [Qb6], and [Nd7], which blocks the c8 bishop, give White most of a pawn. [h5], [b6], [a5], [Nh6], [f6], [Qd7] and [Na6] do little.

Some moves weaken Black seriously. The break [e5] gives a pawn to [e5 dxe5], [b5] and [g5] loosen the position, and [f5] weakens e5 and Black's king. [Kd7] puts the king in front of its pieces, more than three and a half pawns, and [Bh3] gives the bishop away to [Bh3 gxh3].

The shallow search ranks the moves differently. At depth 8 [Nc6] is the best (+0.12) and [Bf5] looks like half a pawn for White (+0.52); at depth 25 [Bf5] is the engine's best (+0.12). [Nd7] goes the other way: +0.39 at depth 8, +0.80 at depth 25, so blocking the bishop costs more than it seems.

The Exchange Caro-Kann structure, one centre pawn each on d4 and d5, with Black's knight on c6 putting pressure on d4. Nothing is attacked yet, and White has a wide choice of moves within a quarter of a pawn of each other.

[c4] is the engine's choice, +0.25: it attacks d5 and gives the game a Panov character, with open lines for White's pieces and an isolated pawn possible on either side. [c3] supports d4 with a pawn, in the spirit of the classical Exchange Variation. [h3], [Ne5], [Be2], [Be3], [Bf4], [Nc3], [Bg5] and [Qd3] are all within a sixth of a pawn of equality.

[Bb5] pins the c6 knight and is about equal (-0.06). [Bd3] is natural but allows [Bd3 Nb4], hitting the bishop, and is rated a little worse, -0.13, like [a4], [a3] and [Nbd2]. [Bd2], [b3], [Na3], [g3], [Qd2] and [Qe2] are a fifth to a third of a pawn behind.

[Ng5], [Ng1], [h4], [b4] and [Rg1] cost about half a pawn, [Nh4] a pawn, and [Ke2] and [Kd2] put the king in the way. [Nfd2] blocks the queen's defence of d4, which falls to [Nfd2 Nxd4], and [g4] gives a pawn to [g4 Bxg4]. Three bishop moves give the bishop away: [Ba6] to [Ba6 bxa6], [Bc4] to [Bc4 dxc4], and [Bh6] to [Bh6 gxh6].

The scores are small and shift with depth. [Nc3] looks like nearly half a pawn for Black at depth 8 and is equal at depth 16 and 25. [Bb5] goes the other way, +0.13 and +0.17 at depths 8 and 16, -0.06 at depth 25. The biggest swing is [Nh4]: three and a half pawns for Black at depth 8, about a pawn deeper.

White's knight is on f3, where it does not defend e4, and White's d-pawn is still on d2. That makes [d5] even more natural than usual: it attacks e4 at once, and the engine gives White only +0.29. After [d5 exd5 cxd5] or [d5 Nc3] the game is a quiet Caro-Kann, and after [d5 e5] White pushes past the attack.

Every other move gives White more than half a pawn. [a6], [d6], [g6], [h6] and [a5] are slow, [e6] and [c5] change the structure without challenging e4, and early queen moves such as [Qa5], [Qc7] and [Qb6] come out before any minor piece. [Nf6] attacks e4 but runs into [Nf6 e5], which chases the knight.

Some moves give a pawn or weaken Black's king. The Gunderam Gambit [e5] loses a pawn to [e5 Nxe5], [b5] to [b5 Bxb5] and [f5] to [f5 exf5]. [f6] takes the knight's square, [h5], [b6], [Nh6] and [Na6] do little, and [g5] drops a pawn to [g5 Nxg5], two and a half pawns for White.

[d5] is the best move at every depth (+0.37, +0.30, +0.29 for White at depths 8, 16 and 25). The move that changes most is [Nf6]: the shallow search gives White a pawn and a half after it, depth 16 only +0.60, and depth 25 settles at +0.85.

Black's d-pawn attacks e4, and the knight on f3 does not defend it. Four moves deal with the threat and keep about a quarter to a third of a pawn, too close for the table to separate. [exd5] exchanges it: after [exd5 cxd5 d4] the game is an Exchange Caro-Kann. The Two Knights [Nc3] defends it with a piece, the advance [e5] pushes it past the attack, and the Endgame Offer [d3] holds it with a pawn, inviting [d3 dxe4 dxe4 Qxd1+] with the queens off.
[Bd3] and [Qe2] defend e4 too, and are about equal: the bishop blocks the d-pawn, and the queen stands in front of the f1 bishop.

Everything else lets Black take on e4, with the f3 knight attacked once the pawn has gone: after [c3 dxe4] or [d4 dxe4] the knight has to move. That costs White between half a pawn and two pawns, from [h4] and [h3], which at least give the knight the h2 square, through [d4], [Ne5], [a4], [c3], [a3], [Nh4], [Be2], [g3], [Nd4], [Na3], [Rg1], [Ng1], [c4], [b3], [Ng5], [b4] and [g4]. [Ke2] gives up castling as well, and three bishop moves give the bishop away: [Bc4 dxc4], [Bb5 cxb5] and [Ba6 Nxa6].

This is a position where the shallow search is easily fooled. [c3] looks fine at depth 8, +0.19, as good as the real defences, but deeper it loses more than a pawn (-1.22 at depth 16, -1.16 at depth 25). [h4] goes the other way, from -1.27 at depth 8 to -0.53. [Nc3] is +0.52 at depth 8 and +0.28 deeper, while [d3] grows from +0.21 to +0.34.

White's pawn stands on d5, and Black is a pawn down. [cxd5] takes it with the c6 pawn and keeps White's edge to +0.21: Black gets a pawn on d5 and an open c-file, and the game goes on with [cxd5 d4] or [cxd5 Bb5+].

[Qxd5] wins the pawn back with the queen, but the queen in the centre is a target, as in [Qxd5 Nc3], and that costs about half a pawn more. Every other move leaves the pawn on d5 for now: [Nf6] can still take it later, but [Qc7], [g6], [h6], [Bg4], [Bf5], [Qb6], [Qa5], [e6], [a6] and the rest give White a pawn or more.
[Kd7] puts the king in front of its pieces, and two bishop moves lose the bishop: [Bh3] to [Bh3 gxh3], and [Be6] to [Be6 dxe6], the d5 pawn taking the bishop.

Here the depths agree: [cxd5] is best at depth 8, 16 and 25, at +0.19 to +0.21 for White, and the order of the rest hardly changes. The only real movers are [Qa5] and [a6], which look about a pawn worse than equal at depth 8 and about a pawn and a half at depth 25.
White has no centre pawn and Black has one on d5. Nothing is attacked, and the position is close to equal whatever White plays: the best moves keep less than a fifth of a pawn.

[d4] is the natural move, staking a claim in the centre and reaching the Exchange Variation's structure, with one pawn each on d4 and d5. [Ne5], the Apocalypse Attack, jumps into the centre at once, and [c3] prepares d4 with a pawn behind it. [Be2], [Nc3], [h3] and [Bb5+] are about equal too, the check being met by ...Nc6 or ...Bd7.

Slower moves cost a little: [b3], [a3], [a4], [d3], [g3], [c4], [Na3], [Bd3] and [Qe2], between a tenth of a pawn and a third. [Nd4], [h4], [b4], [Ng1], [Ng5] and [Rg1] give Black about half a pawn, and [Nh4] more than a pawn.
[Ke2] gives up castling, and [g4] drops a pawn to [g4 Bxg4]. Two bishop moves give the bishop away: [Bc4] to [Bc4 dxc4] and [Ba6] to [Ba6 Nxa6].

The scores are small, but the shallow search ranks them differently. At depth 8 [d4] (+0.15) and [a3] (+0.17) lead, while [c3] looks a little worse than equal (-0.17) and [Ne5] about equal; at depth 16 [c3] is best (+0.26), and at depth 25 [Ne5], [c3] and [d4] share the top at +0.15 to +0.18. [d4] is the steady choice, +0.15 to +0.20 at every depth.
